code.title: ApplicationContext.refresh phases in order

followUps:
The set of bean definitions is frozen: after the BFPP phase Spring calls freezeConfiguration(), so no new definitions can be added or changed. This lets Spring cache merged definitions and resolved metadata and safely start creating singletons without definitions shifting underneath it.

Example: a BPP that tries to registerBeanDefinition after the freeze fails or is ignored. Register extra beans in a BFPP or BeanDefinitionRegistryPostProcessor, not later. Cost: the freeze is O(1); it saves repeated lookups later.

AOT moves the work of reading configuration and conditions to build time. It runs the refresh up to bean definitions, evaluates conditions, and generates plain Java code that registers the definitions, plus reflection, proxy and resource hints for native images.

At runtime there is no classpath scanning, no @Conditional evaluation and no CGLIB generation, so startup is faster and memory lower. The trade-off: profiles and conditions are fixed at build time, so the runtime bean set cannot differ.

Use a SmartInitializingSingleton or listen for ContextRefreshedEvent (or ApplicationReadyEvent in Boot): by then all non-lazy singletons exist and are already wrapped in their proxies.

Do not use @PostConstruct for this: it runs while the context is still being built, so other beans may not exist and proxies are not yet applied. Example: a bean that registers every Handler bean into a router does it in afterSingletonsInstantiated().

code.title: BeanFactoryPostProcessor edits definitions, BeanPostProcessor wraps instances

followUps:
BPPs are sorted into three groups: those implementing PriorityOrdered first, then Ordered, then the rest in registration order; inside a group the lower getOrder() value runs first.

Example: a PriorityOrdered BPP with order 5 runs before an Ordered BPP with order 1. That is why injection and @PostConstruct processors run early, and the auto-proxy creator runs late enough to wrap the finished bean. The same order is used for before-init and after-init calls.

Technically yes, but it is usually a bug: getBean() inside a BFPP instantiates that bean immediately, before the BPPs are registered. The bean then misses injection of @Autowired fields processed by BPPs, misses AOP proxying, and Spring logs "not eligible for getting processed by all BeanPostProcessors".

Edit definitions instead (getBeanDefinition(name).setLazyInit(true)) and leave instance creation to the container.

code.title: Singleton bean lifecycle order

followUps:
Because the transaction advice lives in the proxy, and during @PostConstruct the proxy does not exist yet: it is created in postProcessAfterInitialization, after the init callbacks. The call runs on the raw object.

Fix: run the work later, for example in an ApplicationReadyEvent or SmartInitializingSingleton listener on another bean, or use TransactionTemplate, which needs no proxy.

tx.executeWithoutResult(s -> repo.seed());

It is a callback that runs once, after all non-lazy singletons have been created, which is the safe moment to do work that needs every bean fully built and proxied.

Implement afterSingletonsInstantiated(). Example: a bean that collects all Plugin beans into a registry, or starts a scheduler. Unlike @PostConstruct, other beans are guaranteed to be ready and proxies applied, and it runs once per context, not once per bean.

code.title: Three-level cache resolves a circular dependency

followUps:
Because each cache has a different job: level one holds finished beans, level two holds early references that were already handed out, and level three holds factories that create the early reference on demand.

The factory is needed so an AOP proxy is created only if some other bean actually asks for the early reference. With only two caches, Spring would have to build the proxy eagerly for every bean right after construction, breaking the rule that proxies are made after initialization. The second cache ensures two requesters get the same early object.

Yes: it breaks the cycle by injecting a lazy-resolution proxy instead of the real bean. Spring creates a proxy for the parameter type that resolves the target only on first method call, so the constructor finishes without needing the other bean.

A(@Lazy B b) { this.b = b; }  // b is a proxy
// real B is looked up on first b.use()

Limits: the type must be proxyable (interface or non-final class), and calls in the constructor itself still fail.

code.title: Choosing among several matching beans

followUps:
@Qualifier wins as a filter, and @Primary only breaks ties among what is left. Spring first narrows candidates by the qualifier; a @Primary bean that does not match it is removed.

Example: beans card and paypal (primary); injecting with @Qualifier("card") gives card, even though paypal is primary. Without a qualifier, @Primary picks paypal. So use @Primary for the default and @Qualifier for the explicit exception.

Create your own annotation meta-annotated with @Qualifier, then put it on the bean and on the injection point. It is type-safe and refactor-friendly, unlike a string name.

@Qualifier @Retention(RUNTIME)
@interface Fast {}
@Fast @Bean Pay paypal() {...}
Service(@Fast Pay p) {...}

Add attributes (for example String region()) when you need several dimensions; Spring matches all attribute values.

code.title: @Configuration full mode vs lite mode

followUps:
Because CGLIB works by subclassing and overriding the @Bean method; a final method cannot be overridden, so the interceptor could not run and calls would silently create new objects. Spring fails at startup with a message that the method must not be final.

Same for private methods and a final class. Fix: remove final, or use proxyBeanMethods = false and pass dependencies as method parameters.

A static @Bean method is called without creating the configuration instance at all, and it is not intercepted. Spring calls it directly on the class, so it can run very early.

That is why BFPP and BPP beans must be static: the config class need not be instantiated before BPPs exist, so its @Value and @Autowired fields do not stay null. Cost: it cannot read instance fields, and calling it from another @Bean method creates a new object each time.

code.title: Request-scoped bean behind a singleton proxy

followUps:
Implement a custom Scope that stores instances in a map keyed by the current tenant id, register it with ConfigurableBeanFactory.registerScope("tenant", ...), and use proxyMode = TARGET_CLASS for injection.

get(name, factory) {
  return map.computeIfAbsent(
    TenantContext.id() + name, k -> factory.getObject());
}

The tenant id usually comes from a ThreadLocal filled by a filter. Implement remove() and register destruction callbacks so tenant beans can be cleaned.

Yes: RequestScope registers a destruction callback with the request attributes, so @PreDestroy (and DisposableBean) of a request-scoped bean runs when the request completes. Session scope does the same at session end.

Contrast with prototype beans: the container creates them but never destroys them, so their @PreDestroy is never called. A custom scope must register callbacks itself.

code.title: JDK dynamic proxy with an interceptor chain

followUps:
Spring stacks several advisors by order: lower order number runs first (outermost) on the way in, and last on the way out. Set it with @Order(n) on the aspect class or implement Ordered. Without an order, the sequence is undefined.

Example: @Order(1) security, @Order(2) transaction: security runs, then the transaction starts, then the method, then commit, then security finishes. For two advices in the same aspect, AspectJ precedence rules apply.

Switch to AspectJ when proxies are not enough: you need to advise self-invocation, private or final methods, constructors, field access, or objects not created by Spring.

Use compile-time weaving (ajc) or load-time weaving (a Java agent plus @EnableLoadTimeWeaving) with @EnableTransactionManagement(mode = ASPECTJ). Cost: a more complex build, a slightly harder debugging story; benefit: no proxy overhead and no self-invocation hole.

code.title: Self-invocation bypasses the proxy

followUps:
No. CGLIB subclassing does not help, because Spring's CGLIB proxy is a separate subclass instance that delegates to a different target object; this inside the target is the raw object, not the proxy.

So this.inner() still skips the advice. Only weaving into the class itself with AspectJ, or calling through the proxy, helps.

Write an integration test that starts the Spring context and asserts the advice effect, not just the result. Unit tests with new Service() cannot catch it.

@SpringBootTest class Test {
  @Autowired Service s;
  @Test void inner() {
    s.outer(); // expect an audit/tx effect
    assertTrue(TxSync.wasActive());
  }
}

Assert TransactionSynchronizationManager.isActualTransactionActive() inside the method, or check a counter that the advice increments.

code.title: Transaction bound to the thread

followUps:
Because the transaction is bound to the current thread through a ThreadLocal; an @Async method runs on another thread, which sees no bound connection and starts its own transaction or none at all.

Example: outer tx writes order 1 (uncommitted); the async task on another thread cannot see it and may fail a foreign-key check. Fix: publish the work after commit with @TransactionalEventListener, or put @Transactional on the async method itself.

It is a hint, not a lock: with JPA/Hibernate, readOnly = true sets the session flush mode to MANUAL, so dirty checking and flushing are skipped at commit, and tells the JDBC driver or database the transaction is read-only when supported.

You still can write if you call flush manually, and some databases ignore the hint. Benefit: less memory and CPU for large loaded entity graphs, since snapshots are not compared. It also lets you route to a read replica.

code.title: REQUIRED vs REQUIRES_NEW connections

followUps:
Size the pool so every thread that can hold an outer connection still finds a spare one for the inner: at least threads * (1 + nesting), so with REQUIRES_NEW, two connections per request thread, plus a margin.

Example: 10 request threads, each needing 2, gives 20; a pool of 10 can deadlock, with all 10 holding one and waiting for a second. Better: cap threads below the pool size, or avoid REQUIRES_NEW on hot paths.

The REQUIRES_NEW method simply starts a fresh transaction, because NOT_SUPPORTED had suspended any transaction and left the thread without one. So the inner method runs in its own new transaction on a new connection, independent of the suspended outer one.

Spring suspends only what exists: with NOT_SUPPORTED over an outer tx, it suspends that tx; the nested REQUIRES_NEW then opens another, so one thread can hold two connections.

code.title: After-commit callbacks run only on success

followUps:
Because the AFTER_COMMIT callback runs after the transaction has committed but its resources are still bound to the thread: a plain REQUIRED write would join the finished transaction and never be committed, so the change is silently lost.

Mark the listener's service method @Transactional(propagation = REQUIRES_NEW) so it opens a new transaction that commits on its own. Example: after an order commit, writing an audit row needs its own tx. Reads work without.

The default executor queue capacity is Integer.MAX_VALUE, so the pool never grows beyond core size (8 by default); tasks pile up in an unbounded queue and memory can grow without any rejection.

Set spring.task.execution.pool.queue-capacity to a bounded number (for example 100) and a max size, plus a rejection policy such as CallerRuns, so you get back-pressure instead of an out-of-memory error.

code.title: Auto-configuration backs off for user beans

followUps:
Because @ConditionalOnBean is evaluated while that configuration class is processed, and user configuration order is not guaranteed: the bean you test for may not be registered yet, so the condition gives a wrong answer that can change when classes are reordered.

It is only reliable in auto-configuration, which is deferred until all user beans are known. In your own config prefer @Profile, @ConditionalOnProperty, or @ConditionalOnClass.

A starter is two parts: an auto-configuration module and a thin starter pom that pulls it with its dependencies.

  1. Write a @AutoConfiguration class with @ConditionalOnMissingBean beans and @ConfigurationProperties.
  2. List it in META-INF/spring/org.springframework.boot.autoconfigure.AutoConfiguration.imports.
  3. Make the starter depend on it and the library.

Test with ApplicationContextRunner.

code.title: Property source order and placeholders

followUps:
Highest priority first: @TestPropertySource properties override almost everything except command-line args and test properties attributes; @DynamicPropertySource sits above that, because it is added last to the test environment.

Practical rule: @DynamicPropertySource beats @TestPropertySource, which beats application.properties and environment variables. Use the dynamic one for values only known at runtime, such as a Testcontainers port.

Because @ConfigurationProperties uses Boot's Binder with relaxed rules, while @Value goes through the plain Environment and only gets relaxed matching when you write the key in canonical kebab-case.

Example: @Value("${my.app.max-size}") also finds the env var MY_APP_MAXSIZE (dashes removed, dots become underscores), but @Value("${my.app.maxSize}") does not. Prefer @ConfigurationProperties for groups of settings.
